title: Le tombeau de Couperin (orchestral suite)
hook: Four old French dances, light and clear, each one written in memory of a friend killed in the First World War.

painting.title: The Goatherd
painting.pairingNote: Painted by Gabriel Deluc, the Basque painter to whom Ravel dedicated the Forlane, killed at the front in 1916; a goatherd on the coast at Saint-Jean-de-Luz, across the harbour from Ciboure, where Ravel was born.

facts: A *tombeau*, literally a tomb, was a piece written in memory of someone, a custom of French composers in the 17th century. The Couperin of the title is François Couperin, called “the Great” (1668–1733), harpsichordist to Louis XIV. Ravel said he meant less a tribute to Couperin himself than to French music of that age: its dances, its ornaments, its clarity.

He wrote the suite for piano between 1914 and 1917, in six movements, in the years he served in the war as an army lorry driver. Each movement is dedicated to the memory of friends who had died fighting. When critics found the music too cheerful for a memorial, Ravel answered: “The dead are sad enough, in their eternal silence.”

In 1919 he orchestrated four of the six pieces for a small orchestra (pairs of woodwind, two horns, one trumpet, harp and strings), leaving out the Fugue and the Toccata and putting the Rigaudon last. The orchestral suite was first played in Paris in February 1920 by the Pasdeloup Orchestra under Rhené-Baton.
The oboe is the star: it opens the suite with a stream of rippling notes, sings the Menuet and the slow middle of the Rigaudon.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a rippling prelude for the oboe (I), a lilting, bittersweet dance (II), a gentle minuet with a bagpipe-like middle (III), and a brisk, stamping finale with a pastoral heart (IV).

movements.heading: Prélude
movements.title: Prélude
movements.summary: In memory of Lieutenant Jacques Charlot, who had arranged Ravel’s *Ma mère l’Oye* for solo piano. The oboe sets off at once on a stream of quick, rippling notes that hardly stops for three minutes, passed between the woodwinds and the strings like light on water. It is a [[perpetuum-mobile|perpetuum mobile]], and a famous test for orchestral oboists.

mainIdeas.name: The ripple
mainIdeas.description: a fast, even run of notes in groups of three, decorated with little turns, as in harpsichord music of Couperin’s time.

stops.hear: The oboe alone starts a quick, rippling line over soft strings
Clarinet and flute take turns with the ripple; the oboe answers
stops.happening: The figure travels round the woodwinds

stops.hear: The strings join in; the harmony shifts into new, brighter colours
stops.happening: The music moves away from home

stops.hear: The oboe’s opening returns

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The ripple climbs and the music ends with a quick, bright flourish

notice: Listen for the moments the oboe hands the ripple to another instrument. The line never breaks; only the colour changes.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The oboe soloist is Robert Casier, credited on the album.

movements.heading: Forlane
movements.title: Forlane
movements.summary: In memory of Gabriel Deluc, a Basque painter from Saint-Jean-de-Luz. The [[forlane|forlane]] is an old Italian dance in a lilting six-beat rhythm; Ravel prepared for this piece by copying out a forlane by Couperin. Ravel’s version keeps the old rhythm but adds harmonies that sound slightly sour, as if remembered through a clouded glass. A refrain keeps coming back between gentler episodes.

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: a lilting tune with a limping, dotted rhythm and bittersweet, clashing chords.

mainIdeas.name: The episodes
mainIdeas.description: smoother, more tender music between the returns of the refrain.

stops.hear: A lilting dance tune with a skipping rhythm, its chords a little sour
The music turns smoother and gentler
The skipping refrain is back
A new, more tender melody
The refrain once more, with fuller scoring
Quieter, more distant music
The refrain a last time, fading

notice: Listen to the harmony under the refrain. The rhythm is an old dance, but the chords belong to 1917.

movements.heading: Menuet
movements.title: Menuet
movements.summary: In memory of Jean Dreyfus, at whose home Ravel recovered after leaving the army. The oboe sings a graceful minuet tune over a light accompaniment. In the middle comes a [[musette|musette]], music in imitation of a bagpipe: a low held note underneath and a hushed, solemn tune that slowly grows to a powerful climax, before the minuet returns.

mainIdeas.name: The minuet
mainIdeas.description: a calm, elegant tune for the oboe in three-beat time.

mainIdeas.name: The musette
mainIdeas.description: a [[drone|drone]] in the low instruments and a quiet tune that swells to a climax.

stops.hear: The oboe sings a gentle, graceful tune over light strings
The tune passes to other wind instruments and the strings
stops.happening: The minuet repeated in new colours

stops.hear: A low note held underneath; a hushed, solemn melody above
The music swells to a full, glowing climax
The oboe’s minuet returns, with the musette tune woven in

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Soft, high chords; the dance fades

notice: In the middle section, listen for the low note that never moves. Above it, everything grows; below it, nothing changes.

movements.heading: Rigaudon
movements.title: Rigaudon
movements.summary: In memory of Pierre and Pascal Gaudin, two brothers who were Ravel’s childhood friends, killed by the same shell in November 1914. A [[rigaudon|rigaudon]] is a lively old dance from the south of France. The orchestra stamps it out with bright, brisk energy; in the middle the oboe slows down for a wistful, pastoral tune over plucked strings, like a guitar. Then the brisk dance returns and the suite ends.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: loud, quick and sharply accented, in C major.

mainIdeas.name: The middle
mainIdeas.description: a slower, pastoral melody for the oboe in C minor, over [[pizzicato|pizzicato]] strings.

stops.hear: The full orchestra bursts in with a brisk, stamping dance
Lighter, but still quick and bright
Slower: the oboe sings a wistful melody over plucked strings
stops.happening: The middle section, in C minor

stops.hear: The melody passes to other wind instruments
The brisk opening returns at full strength

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A quick final flourish and a sharp last chord

notice: Notice the contrast inside this short piece: noise and bustle on both sides, and in the middle a tune that sounds almost like a lament.

threads.title: Memory without mourning
threads.body: Each piece remembers someone killed in the war, but none is a lament. Ravel’s answer was that the dead are sad enough; the music offers them clear, bright dances instead.

threads.title: Old forms, new harmony
threads.body: Prélude, forlane, minuet and rigaudon were all dances of Couperin’s time. Ravel keeps their shapes and rhythms and fills them with harmonies of his own day, an early example of [[neoclassicism|neoclassicism]].

threads.title: Piano first
threads.body: Like much of Ravel’s music, the suite exists twice, for piano and for orchestra. In the orchestral version the piano’s six pieces become four.
